co_mt_blue_sky_formerly_mount_evans_mixe.skip_reason: Only page is the author's own account of using it as a descent through a cornice; no second source and no approach or top-out detail.

set.approach: The summit road (Highway 5) is seasonal and closed in winter, so in the cold months the approach adds a long walk up the road or in from Echo Lake via the Chicago Lakes basin. From the Summit Lake parking area, the Crystal is a narrowing couloir below the northwest face, just right of The Snave. It sits in morning shade, so the snow stays firm longer than on the sunnier couloirs of the bowl. Crampons and an axe are the standard kit. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single route page for location; descent not set because only a ski descent is described.

co_mt_blue_sky_formerly_mount_evans_mixe.skip_reason: Page does not say whether it was climbed or descended, and the exit described (Chicago Lakes basin vs Summit Lake trail) is ambiguous; single source.

set.approach: The summit road (Highway 5) is seasonal and closed in winter, so in the cold months the approach adds a long walk up the road or in from Echo Lake via the Chicago Lakes basin. From the Summit Lake parking area, walk to the east end of the lake and climb into the Summit Lake bowl. The snowfield is straight ahead, a broad slope between The Snave and the Diamond Couloir, and it is not always continuous up to the ridge. It is moderate snow, with crampons and an axe. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page and ski guide agree on the bowl approach from Summit Lake. Top-out not stated, so no descent.

co_ne_buttress_hallett_peak_mixed_ice_ha.skip_reason: No page found for this route; it is only mentioned as a descent for The Cleft.

set.approach: Start at the Bear Lake trailhead and take the trail to Emerald Lake, roughly 1.7 to 1.8 miles one way. At the shore, look left for the climbers' trail, then climb it up and right, contouring above the lake to the base of the big rock buttresses. Continue along the cliff base, then turn right and work up the gorge, staying slightly left of its middle to the obvious base of the couloir. The approach to the end of Tyndall Gorge is long. Snow slopes below the face can slide, so check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page and area page agree on the trail; summit is a short walk from the top but no descent is stated, so omitted.

set.approach: The couloir starts from the Bottomless Pit below the north face. Three ways in are used: the long hike up the Barr Trail, a shorter but harder hike from the Crags trailhead, or a short descent from the toll road, which leaves no easy way back down. The Hero Traverse from the toll road also reaches the foot of the line. The line is obvious to the south; start up the main gully, and the Y branches west, to climber's right, after about a third of a mile.

review.notes: Route page for the three approaches and the branching; Guide's Couloir page confirms Hero Traverse access. Descent from the summit not described, so omitted.

set.approach: From the Glacier Gorge side, follow the route toward Andrews Glacier and turn left into The Gash, the hanging valley between the glacier and Sharkstooth. A broad cliff band with a notch through its middle crosses the head of the valley, and the couloir lies there. Start at the right-hand end of the lower 50-foot cliff band, which is the shorter way in; the narrowest, steepest part of the couloir is not far above that cliff. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The couloir ends on the ridge above a broad, fan-shaped headwall, and a large cornice often guards the top into spring. Exiting left avoids the cornice. From the crest, turn north (right) to Andrews Glacier and descend it to the Andrews Glacier trail. The glacier is a snow slope that firms up to ice late in the year, so carry an axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Couloir page gives the line, approach and walk-off; glacier page confirms ice later in the season. No counts used.

set.approach: Follow the Andrews Glacier route toward Andrews Tarn and turn left into The Gash, heading for Sharkstooth. The gully is on the west side of the spire as seen from The Gash, and the line climbed runs in the right-hand gully right next to the spire; a few variations lie to the right (west). It is a short but steep gully rather than a distinct couloir, so it is easy to wander past. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Location text of both Gash routes agrees on the Andrews Glacier turn-off into The Gash. Descent not stated; not written.

co_andrews_creek_the_gash_andrews_glacie.skip_reason: Only one readable page, with no approach and no description of where the glacier ends; trail details seen only in search summaries were not read.

set.approach: From the Brainard Lake area start at the Long Lake trailhead and follow the Pawnee Pass trail past Long Lake to Lake Isabelle, then continue west along the Isabelle Glacier trail to the tarn below Navajo, Apache and Shoshoni peaks. The road to the Long Lake trailhead is seasonal and can add miles on foot in spring. Cross the Isabelle Glacier to its southwest corner, where the route climbs a steep snow ramp to a saddle below the summit. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: MP route gives the Lake Isabelle and glacier line; ski guide gives the trailhead, trail, tarn and seasonal road. Descent not stated for foot parties; not written.

set.approach: Start at the Fourth of July trailhead above Eldora and take the trail to the Fourth of July Mine. At the mine take the right fork toward the couloir; where the trail turns east up the hillside, leave it and strike due north up the slope to the foot of the couloir that cuts the south side of South Arapahoe Peak. It begins at roughly 40 degrees and steepens toward the top, and the direct finish is steeper. Indian Peaks permits apply to some overnight trips. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: MP and CMC agree on the Fourth of July trailhead; MP gives the mine and fork. No sourced descent route; counts left out.

set.approach: Use the Skywalker Couloir approach from the Fourth of July trailhead: the trail to the Fourth of July Mine, the right fork toward the couloirs, then north across the hillside. Streetwalker is the rightmost finger of snow, about 200 yards right of Skywalker. It resembles the lower part of Skywalker, with easy to moderate snow. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Streetwalker page places it relative to Skywalker, whose page gives the approach. Descent not stated; not written.

set.approach: Leave Bear Lake on the Flattop trail, bound for Lake Helene. Shortly before the main path bends right toward Odessa Lake, a faint climbers' path on the left drops through the trees to the lake. Continue above the lake to the tarn below Notchtop. From the tarn, climb the snowfield on the Notchtop side (climber's right) so that the gully and its branches stay in view; hugging the Flattop side hides them. The start is obvious. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The gully is tight and winding and ends at the summit of Flattop Mountain. From there either hike the Flattop trail back to Bear Lake or glissade the Ptarmigan snowfields and walk out the way you came. Any short rock steps partway up are easily scrambled over, and the last few feet can be noticeably steeper than the rest, so carry an axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Gully page gives tarn, snowfield side and summit exit with walk-off; Ptarmigan page gives the Bear Lake to Lake Helene trail. Distances left out.

set.approach: Leave Bear Lake on the Flattop trail, bound for Lake Helene. Just before the main path bends right toward Odessa Lake, a faint climbers' path on the left leads down through the trees to the lake. The gully starts from the south side of the lake and is the farthest left of the snow climbs on Flattop. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The gully runs between two rock buttresses near the top and ends on the summit of Flattop Mountain, with some easy mixed scrambling possible between snowfields. Descend by the Flattop trail back toward Bear Lake. Carry an axe and crampons for the snow. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Northeast Gully page: start at Lake Helene, tops out on summit, descend Flattop Trail. Approach trail from the Ptarmigan page.

set.approach: Leave Bear Lake on the Flattop trail, bound for Lake Helene. Just before the main path bends right toward Odessa Lake, a faint climbers' path on the left descends gently through the trees to the lake; pass it on its right-hand shore. Stay on the path and cairns, or the easiest line when snow covers them, to the foot of a snowfield at the south end of the base of Notchtop Spire. That is the lower glacier. From its top, bear up and a little right to reach the foot of the steeper upper glacier. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single page, specific trail directions. Descent not described; not written.

set.approach: The couloir looks toward Telluride, yet the simplest way in is from the Yankee Boy Basin side, to the north. Take the Camp Bird road from Ouray as far as it is plowed or passable toward the lower Sneffels trailhead, then walk up the road and turn southwest a short way past the toilets. Cross the rolling ground on the west flank of Stony Mountain, aiming at the saddle between Emma and Gilpin that closes the basin, cross over, and traverse northwest below the outcrops of Gilpin's south ridge, holding about the 12,400-foot contour to the bench below the southwest face. You can't miss the couloir from that bench. While the Camp Bird road remains shut for winter, the approach from Mill Creek west of Telluride may be shorter, though conditions may not yet be right. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: Where the inset corridor ends on the upper southwest face, a final stretch of snow or loose rock leads to the summit. Most parties not skiing descend the northwest ridge and then the standard gully into Yankee Boy Basin, where the steepest snow of a spring day is often found. The saddle between Gilpin and Block Tops also offers a gully running south toward Mill Creek. Carry an axe, crampons and a helmet. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single detailed route page. Counts left out. Search listings showed no second description.

set.approach: Start from the Glen Cove area on the Pikes Peak toll road, which is a seasonal road. From George's Corner, the usual starting point for these lines, go north up an old drainage. Where it opens into the big pit, angle right across the slope until the line appears in front of you. It is a north-facing line, and conditions are usually best from mid-spring into early summer. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: Ski down, or walk down by way of the Big Blue slope to the east. Carry an axe and check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Both pages from the same area agree on the start point and descent via Big Blue. Elevations left out.

set.approach: Start from the Glen Cove area on the Pikes Peak toll road, which is a seasonal road. From George's Corner walk north up the drainage to a clearing or pit, then work along the edge of the pit heading north; the couloir is straight ahead. It faces north. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: Ski down, or walk down by way of the Big Blue slope to the east. The couloir can hide rocks that make a ski descent hazardous unless it is well filled in. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Chimney and Little Italy pages agree on the Big Blue walk-off.

set.approach: Park at the switchback on the right side of the Pikes Peak toll road above Glen Cove (the road is seasonal and tolled). Walk up into the cirque under the north face, above Glen Cove, and over to the foot of the Three Little Pigs system, the W-shaped set of couloirs along the east wall of the cirque. This line is the furthest left couloir. The approach is short. Higher up, the route passes through some easy broken terraces to reach the upper ramparts. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single page. Descent not stated; not written.

set.approach: Begin at the parking pullouts at Cove Creek on the Pikes Peak toll road, just past the gift shop and the brake check station. The route is the north-facing snow slope above that area. The road is seasonal. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: Because the toll road crosses the slope at the bottom and again at the top, a car shuttle is easy, and the slope is most often used by skiers and snowboarders. The upper end is on the road, so you can finish there. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single short page. Elevations left out.

set.approach: From George's Corner on the Pikes Peak toll road (a seasonal road), head southwest up the east-facing bowl. A large cornice guards the top, and it has released an avalanche that ran to the road in the past; most parties stay on the climber's right (south) side to avoid the hazard above. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single short page. Descent not stated.

set.approach: Start at the Grizzly trailhead and follow the easy trail up to Grizzly Lake; most of it is fairly flat and the route is hard to lose. Circle the lake, then climb talus to the big snow couloir that drops to the right of the summit. Snow climbing begins somewhere above 12,600 feet depending on conditions. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The couloir tops out a short scramble from the summit and steepens as you climb, to around 45 to 50 degrees near the top. Either walk down the west slopes to the road, or glissade and downclimb the couloir with great care. Rocks fall from the cliffs on either side, so wear a helmet. A fall high up could slide a long way, though the angle eases a lot near the bottom. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single page for this couloir (Sawatch Grizzly Peak matches the coordinates). Mileage left out.

set.approach: Reach Chaos Canyon from the Bear Lake side by the trail to Lake Haiyaha, which leaves the Dream Lake trail. Early in the season that route can be icy and deep in snow, so another option is an unofficial path that begins close to where the Mills Lake and Loch trails split. From the left side of Lake Haiyaha pick the easiest way up the canyon, over boulders, to the base of the couloir, which becomes obvious as you gain ground. An alternate start climbs the gully south of Emerald Lake to the east ridge and then scrambles around the south side of the ridge, just under the cliffs, to the upper half of the couloir. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The couloir curves up Hallett's east ridge. At the top you can downclimb it or follow the wide, rocky ridge to the summit, which takes a last short climb on the summit snowfield. The easiest way down from the summit is the Flattop trail; Tyndall Gorge is another way. The couloir is steeper in its upper half. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single page. Approach distances left out. A second source (SummitPost) was blocked from reading, so it is not listed.

set.approach: From the St. Mary's Glacier trailhead walk the steep road to St. Mary's Lake, go around its north side, and climb the glacier to the plain of Jamaica Flats. Head west up the southeast slopes of James Peak to roughly 12,750 feet, then cross over the head of the Bailout ski route and drop north into the basin beneath the east face. Do not descend Bailout itself. The route begins by following the lower part of Starlight Couloir, then angles right into a steeper couloir that runs parallel to it. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page gives line and exit onto SE ridge; ski guide gives trailhead, Jamaica Flats, Bailout and the SE slopes as the moderate route. Walk back down the SE slopes is inferred from the ski guide describing them as the approach.

set.approach: Start at the Fourth of July trailhead and follow the Arapaho Pass trail about a mile to a fork, then take the Diamond Lake trail down to Middle Boulder Creek and on to Diamond Lake and Upper Diamond Lake. The route is on the southeast face of Jasper Peak, climber's right of a broken rock rib that comes down from the summit. The slope begins gently and steepens at a constriction and again near the ridge crest. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The northeast slopes route is an easy way down from the summit, and sliding down the neighbouring Gaiteraid couloir returns to the base of Snow Lion. The top of Snow Lion can be steep and rotten after the sun reaches it, and cornices may form on the ridge. Carry an axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page gives the base and descent; ski guide confirms trailhead, trail and creek. Counts left out.

set.approach: Start at the Fourth of July trailhead and follow the Arapaho Pass trail about a mile to the fork, then take the Diamond Lake trail down to Middle Boulder Creek and on toward Diamond Lake. The couloir is centred on the east face of Jasper Peak, between Snow Lion and the Gaiteraid couloir. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: Come down by the Gaiteraid couloir, or look for easier ground further east on Jasper's east ridge. The upper part is steeper than Snow Lion, with a near-vertical or overhanging last few feet, and the summit cornice may only melt out late in the season. The crux gets early sun, so start early and watch for rockfall. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page for line, neighbours and descents; ski guide for trailhead and trail. Counts left out.

set.approach: This is a full day's approach, so most parties camp at Mirror Lake or push on and camp near Triangle Lake closer to the base. Cross the outlet of Mirror Lake and head up Cascade Creek, then scramble up to Triangle Lake. Hike around its west side; the glacier rises ahead in the headwall of the little cirque. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page gives the camp, creek, lake and route; ski guide confirms Fair Glacier lies west of Apache. Trailhead not stated in sources read; descent not stated.

set.approach: Park at the Glacier Gorge Junction trailhead and follow signs past the lakes to Black Lake. Cross the lake at its outlet boulders and follow the east side up. Scramble over talus and ledges to the snow; the Trough is the longest finger of snow reaching into the northwest face of the peak, and it is visible from much of the hike after Black Lake. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The snow meets the Keyhole route at the Narrows, where parties continue to the summit by the Homestretch; leave the pack at the top of the snow if you are going on. Descend by ski, glissade or crampons down the Trough, or reverse the Keyhole route through the boulderfield back toward Bear Lake. Rocks fall from the Keyhole route above, and the snow can be unstable, so wear a helmet and check the forecast. Carry an axe and crampons.

review.notes: Single detailed route page. Distances and times left out.

set.approach: Start at the Glacier Gorge trailhead and follow the trail past Mills Lake and Black Lake to Green Lake, which is ringed by Spearhead, Chiefs Head, Pagoda and Longs. The couloir rises to the saddle between the Keyboard of the Winds and Pagoda and is longer than it looks; the slabs near its foot shed wet slides, and the line may need to cut left at the bottom to avoid them. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single page. Descent not given; not written.

set.approach: Begin at the Fourth of July trailhead and walk to Arapaho Pass via the mine, then angle south and west past the east and south shores of Lake Dorothy and into the cirque on Neva's northeast side. Juliet is the southernmost of the couloirs cutting the face, one or two couloirs to the left of one that has a cornice. The face is a popular one, so watch for parties above. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The north ridge is a possible way down and is Class 4, so a light rack and slings may be useful. The northeast slopes, the most moderate line on this face, are another option. Check for cornices and parties above before dropping in. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page gives approach and north ridge descent; ski guide confirms the line and the northeast slopes as the moderate route. Distances left out.

set.approach: Start at the Mitchell Lake trailhead, reached from Brainard Lake; the road beyond the gateway is closed seasonally, which adds distance in spring. Follow the Mitchell Lake trail past the lake to Blue Lake and cross it, usually frozen early, then climb a series of plateaus from the southwest corner into the bowl below the south face. Zigzag up the bowl, bearing right toward the saddle where the south ridge begins. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The south face and its bowl are the easiest way to the summit and also the standard way down from the technical lines, retracing the approach through the bowl and over the plateaus to Blue Lake. The slope is wide with safe runouts. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page and ski guide agree on Mitchell Lake trail to Blue Lake and the bowl. Mileages differ between sources and are left out.

set.approach: Begin at the Mitchell Lake trailhead, off the Brainard Lake road, and take the Blue Lake trail; the trail may be snow covered, and the road is seasonal. Pass the lake on its north shore and climb the couloir, which is out of sight until you are close. Several snow strips may show; pick the westernmost one that stays unbroken longest. It is not deeply inset, and it bends west in the middle. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The couloir tops out at a shallow saddle on the ridge toward Paiute Peak, a short walk from the summit. The bend means a skier cannot follow the fall line, and a slip could slam you into the side walls. The couloir is also skied back to Blue Lake, and in late spring it melts out into scree. Carry an axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page and ski guide agree on the Blue Lake approach and the north-side start. Descent is the route itself (ski or reverse) and the saddle top-out; no separate walk-off is stated.

set.approach: The approach is the hard part of this route. The first ascent party went from the Mitchell Lake trailhead partway up Mt. Audubon, then north down from a saddle on Audubon's east ridge and traversing its north face, which was slow and somewhat risky. Two better options are suggested: continue over Audubon's summit to the Audubon-Paiute col, then drop down steep snow more directly to the foot of the northeast face (crampons and axes needed); or drop from the east-ridge saddle on steep snow to Upper Coney Lake and follow the drainage up to the face. The couloir is the central line on the big northeast face. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single route account for the approaches; ski guide confirms the Mitchell Lake trailhead. No descent stated. Times left out.

set.approach: Two approaches are used. The short one drives the Camp Bird road toward Yankee Boy Basin, as far as the plowed or rough road allows (around the lower Sneffels trailhead or somewhat beyond), then goes up the hillside to the north and contours east, staying over the cliffs, to the grass below the Potosi-Coffeepot saddle. Gain the saddle by talus, drop steeply down the north side, ideally on snow, and then cross east to reach the couloir's foot. The longer one starts at the Weehawken trailhead on the Camp Bird road, follows the trail and then contours into Weehawken Creek and up the drainage to the north face; it is long but scenic and easier to route-find. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: From the top-out, either bear right up the snowfield to the summit, or work down the gully to the south until the ledges to the west allow a scramble back up. The exit is seldom corniced, though it can be steeper on the right. Come down by the standard summer southeast gully, or ski back down. If you came in via Yankee Boy Basin, go west at about 13,300 feet along the upper ramp to the southwest corner, then traverse the west face on social trails back to the saddle. If you came via Weehawken Creek, go east at 13,300 feet and downclimb the southeast ridge, then follow the drainage northeast. Carry an axe, crampons and a helmet. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Single detailed page. Distances left out. Search listings agreed with the two approaches.

set.approach: Start at the Blue Lakes trailhead and follow the trail upstream and across the creek before the two-mile mark. Turn right into the brush and bushwhack up the left side of the creek to the north face of S6. The couloir is the east (looker's left) line on that face, with 30-degree ice and snow on rolling moraines at the bottom. Beware of rockfall from the rotten walls. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The couloir tops out below the summit on the east ridge, and a short, easy scramble leads to the top. Descend the way you came or take another route. The top is steep for a short stretch and may need a cornice crossing late in the season. Carry a helmet, axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Both S6 pages give the Blue Lakes start; the Lotion page the line and exit. Distances left out.

set.approach: From the Blue Lakes trailhead take the Blue Lakes trail (#201) south for less than two miles to an obvious creek crossing, then leave the trail and follow the creek west, staying on the south side to a large clearing near 10,500 feet. Then cross to the north bank and keep to it until the creek swings southwest, and follow the creek bed, which is usually snow filled. After a steep rise the basin stretches southwest. Head for the north buttress of S6 and go right around the north spur to reach the couloir hidden behind it. The route is the one on the opposite side of the buttress from the northeast couloir. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The couloir joins the ridge, often with a cornice that is easy to bypass; walk a short way east to the high point. Options down: go over the summit east and descend the northeast couloir from the first saddle, which is usually steep for a few metres at the top; continue further east, drop onto the south face by easy Class 3 ground (normally cairned) to the notch of the S6-S5 saddle, and descend the northeast-facing couloir there; or reverse the north couloir. Carry a helmet, axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: North and Directissimo pages agree on the approach and shared descents. Counts left out.

set.approach: From the Blue Lakes trailhead take the Blue Lakes trail (#201) south for less than two miles to an obvious creek crossing, then leave the trail and follow the creek west, staying on the south side to a large clearing near 10,500 feet. Then cross to the north bank and keep to it until the creek swings southwest, and follow the creek bed. After a steep rise the basin stretches southwest; look for the prominent couloir along the east edge of the north face. The line starts up the northeast couloir and branches right higher up. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The line ends on the ridge about 50 yards west of the summit; a massive cornice often guards the headwall, or there may be no snow at all, and the fallback is the narrow chute along the right wall, or the main couloir. The simplest way down is the main northeast couloir from east of the summit. Other descents are those used for the north couloir. Rockfall can be an issue, so start early and wear a helmet. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Two pages agree on approach and descents.

set.approach: Leave the car at either pullout beside the Rock Cut, on the seasonal Trail Ridge Road in Rocky Mountain National Park. A short, easy hike gaining roughly 300 to 500 feet takes you to the summit, above the tops of the couloirs, where you can check the cornices before dropping into the basin on the north side. The couloirs are visible once you are in the basin, and the easiest, a wider line, tops out in a notch just northwest of the summit. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: Walk back out over the summit hike to the Trail Ridge Road turnouts. Another way is to descend the easiest couloir, about 700 feet, or to walk a quarter to half mile east to easy snow or talus slopes. The top of the couloirs can be guarded by a cornice. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page, area page and CMC agree on the turnout approach and the summit hike gain (range of 300 to 500 feet); descent options from the area page.

set.approach: Follow the Stevens Gulch trail from the Grays Peak trailhead toward the east face of Torreys and drop into the basin when you are directly opposite the couloir. Trudge up the runout into the main couloir, which is the main line on the east face. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The upper couloir averages about 45 degrees and ends some 150 to 200 feet under the summit, so scramble the rest of the way up. Descend the south ridge to the low saddle between Torreys and Grays, then glissade or downclimb into the basin, or follow the trail down from the saddle. Stones come off the upper walls once the sun warms them, so wear a helmet. Carry an axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Dead Dog page for approach and top-out; South Paw page for the col and trail descent. Counts left out because gain figures differ between sources.

set.approach: Use the Grays Peak trailhead and follow the trail toward the Grays and Torreys route; in winter the road is gated at the I-70 exit, making for a long day. Roughly a mile up, at the Grays Peak sign, turn west down Grizzly Gulch to reach the Tuning Fork, a long strip of snow on Torreys' northwest face, visible from the interstate. The standard route to the saddle and summit crosses avalanche paths, and the face can be climbed directly as a difficult Class 2 snow climb. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: Route page and ski-line page agree on the Grays Peak trailhead, the saddle and southeast ridge standard route, and that the face is climbable. Walk-off from the top is inferred as the standard route reversed.

set.descent_text: The gully meets the ridge south of Torreys' summit, close to the trail linking Grays and Torreys. Descend by reversing the route, or climb the last 350 feet to the summit and take the Kelso Ridge down, or head south to the saddle and take the trail down, or go up to Grays Peak and walk down its trail. A standing wave or small serac near the top can be passed on the left or lower, depending on conditions. Carry an axe and crampons. Check the avalanche forecast first.

review.notes: South Paw page gives the descent options; Dead Dog page confirms the saddle and Kelso side. Approach not stated; not written.

set.approach: From CO 145, take either the Navajo Lake trail (#635) south of Telluride or the Rock of Ages trail (#429) west of Telluride. Navajo Lake is slightly longer but has better camping and gives a preview of the route and its conditions. From the lake or the Rock of Ages area, head for El Diente's north face. The line lies immediately west of the North Buttress; climb the talus right under the buttress and then step right into the couloir. When it is in condition the snow reaches 12,300 feet or lower, so no scrambling on the buttress is needed. These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
set.descent_text: The route climbs the northwest couloir directly to the summit of El Diente. The usual way down continues the traverse to Mount Wilson (Class 3 to 4) and descends its north slopes. Rockfall and the hanging snowfield near the top call for a helmet, axe and crampons, and for timing so the snow is not too soft there. Check the avalanche forecast first.
